title: The Third Declension — Consonant Stems
subtitle: rēx, lūx, miles, pater, soror. The genitive reveals the stem.
objectives: Decline third-declension consonant-stem nouns in all cases.
Recognize that the genitive singular reveals the stem.
Understand that third-declension nouns can be masculine, feminine, or neuter.
Translate sentences with third-declension nouns as subjects and objects.

sections.heading: The third declension: consonant stems
sections.body:
The third declension is the largest and most varied. Nouns can be masculine, feminine, or neuter. The nominative singular can end in almost any letter. The genitive singular always ends in -is, and reveals the stem.

Paradigm: rēx, rēgis (king, masc.):

          Singular    Plural
  Nom.    rēx         rēgēs
  Gen.    rēgis       rēgum
  Dat.    rēgī        rēgibus
  Acc.    rēgem       rēgēs
  Abl.    rēge        rēgibus

The stem is rēg-. The nominative singular (rēx) is formed by adding -s, which causes the g to become x (g + s → x).

Caesar writes: mīles fortis. — A brave soldier.
Cicero writes: pater patriae. — Father of the fatherland.

sections.heading: Common third-declension nouns
sections.body:
miles, militis (m.) — soldier
pater, patris (m.) — father
māter, mātris (f.) — mother
soror, sorōris (f.) — sister
lūx, lūcis (f.) — light
vōx, vōcis (f.) — voice
nōmen, nōminis (n.) — name
corpus, corporis (n.) — body

items.prompt: Decline dux, ducis (leader, m.) in the singular.
What does the genitive singular of a third-declension noun tell you?
items.answer: The stem, to which you add the other case endings.
